subject: math
title: Grade 9 Budgets and Transactions: Pay, Fixed and Variable Expenses, GST and PST, Bank Fees and Saving Goals
seo_title: Grade 9 Budgets and Transactions Worksheets: Net Pay, Budgets, GST + PST and Bank Fees (Free, Answer Key, BC Curriculum)
standard_text: Financial literacy – simple budgets and transactions
meta_desc: Free Grade 9 math worksheets on budgets and transactions for the BC curriculum: hourly wages, gross and net pay, fixed and variable expenses, 5% GST and 7% PST, bank balances and fees, and saving goals. 100 questions with an answer key.
key_big: Income − expenses = what you can save. Add 12% tax (5% GST + 7% PST) to most prices before you plan.
key_sub: Net pay is gross pay minus deductions. Fixed expenses stay the same each month; variable expenses change. Subtract every fee from a bank balance, and round the weeks to a saving goal up.
body_html:
Income: gross pay and net pay

For an hourly job, gross pay = hourly wage × hours. Your employer then takes off deductions: income tax, CPP (Canada Pension Plan) and EI (Employment Insurance). What is left is your net pay, the money you take home.

Change minutes to hours before you multiply: 7 hours 30 minutes is 7.5 hours, not 7.3 hours.

Budgets: fixed and variable expenses

A budget compares money in (income) with money out (expenses). A fixed expense is the same each month, like rent or a phone plan. A variable expense changes, like food, gas or fun. Income − expenses gives a surplus (left over) or a deficit (short).

Example

Income is $1500 a month. Fixed expenses are $900. Variable expenses are $420. How much can be saved?

Expenses: $900 + $420 = $1320. Surplus: $1500 − $1320 = $180.

Answer: $180 a month

Transactions with GST and PST

Most things you buy in BC have 5% GST and 7% PST added, 12% in total. Children’s clothing and restaurant meals have GST only. Take any discount first, then add the tax. Cash totals round to the nearest 5¢; debit and credit are exact.

Bank balances and fees

Deposits are added. Withdrawals, purchases and fees are subtracted. Keep a running balance, one row at a time. A balance below zero is written with a minus sign, like −$25.00.

Saving goals

Weeks needed = amount still needed ÷ amount saved each week. If the answer is not a whole number, round up, because you cannot buy the item until the full amount is saved.

Example

A $250 bike has 12% tax. You save $30 a week. How many weeks?

Total: $250 × 1.12 = $280. $280 ÷ $30 = 9.33..., so round up.

Answer: 10 weeks

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Forgetting to add GST and PSTMultiply the price by 1.12 (or add 5% GST only for children’s clothing and restaurant meals)
Calling a bill “fixed” because you pay it every monthFixed means the amount stays the same; a bill that changes is variable
Mixing up gross and net payNet pay = gross pay − deductions
7 h 30 min = 7.3 hours30 minutes = 0.5 hour, so 7.5 hours
Forgetting bank fees in a balanceSubtract every fee, like a withdrawal
Rounding the number of weeks downRound up so the full amount is saved

faq.q: What is the difference between fixed and variable expenses?
faq.a: A fixed expense costs the same each month, like rent, a phone plan or a transit pass. A variable expense changes from month to month, like groceries, gas, electricity or entertainment.

faq.q: What is the difference between gross pay and net pay?
faq.a: Gross pay is what you earn before deductions, such as hourly wage × hours. Net pay is what you take home after income tax, CPP and EI are taken off.

faq.q: How do you add GST and PST to a price in BC?
faq.a: Most items have 5% GST and 7% PST, so multiply the price by 1.12. A $50 item costs $50 × 1.12 = $56; children’s clothing and restaurant meals have only the 5% GST.

faq.q: What do Grade 9 students learn about financial literacy in BC?
faq.a: The BC Mathematics 9 curriculum includes simple budgets and transactions. Students work out pay, build budgets with fixed and variable expenses, add sales tax, track bank balances and plan saving goals.

sets.title: Income: wages, gross pay and net pay

items.q: Wei earns $18.00 an hour at a grocery store in Surrey. He works 20 hours this week. What is his gross pay?
items.e: Gross pay = hourly wage × hours = $18.00 × 20 = $360.00. ($38.00 adds instead of multiplying; $342.00 uses 19 hours.)

items.q: What is gross pay?
c: Only the money taken off for income tax
Pay after the deductions are taken off
Pay before any deductions are taken off
Only the pay for overtime hours
items.e: Gross pay is everything you earn before deductions. Net pay (take-home pay) is what is left after deductions.

items.q: A pay stub shows gross pay of $600.00 and deductions of $90.00. What is the net pay?
items.e: Net pay = gross pay − deductions = $600.00 − $90.00 = $510.00. ($690.00 adds the deductions; $600.00 is the gross pay.)

items.q: Which amounts are usually taken off a paycheque in Canada?
items.e: Employers take off income tax, CPP (Canada Pension Plan) and EI (Employment Insurance). GST and PST are sales taxes you pay when you buy things, not paycheque deductions.

items.q: Leah earns $17.50 an hour and works 24 hours. What is her gross pay?
Chloe works a shift of 7 hours 30 minutes at $18.00 an hour. How much does she earn for the shift?
items.e: 30 minutes is half an hour, so the shift is 7.5 hours (not 7.3). $18.00 × 7.5 = $135.00. ($131.40 uses 7.3 hours; $126.00 forgets the 30 minutes.)

items.q: Owen works 4 hours on Monday, 3.5 hours on Wednesday and 6.5 hours on Saturday at $18.50 an hour. What is his gross pay?
Gross pay is $800.00. Deductions are 20% of gross pay. What is the net pay?
items.e: Deductions: 20% of $800 = $160. Net pay: $800 − $160 = $640.00. ($160.00 is the deductions; $780.00 subtracts 20 dollars, not 20%.)

items.q: In BC, overtime is usually paid at time and a half: 1.5 times the regular wage. What is the overtime rate for a $20.00 hourly wage?
items.e: Time and a half = 1.5 × $20.00 = $30.00 an hour. ($40.00 is double time; $21.50 adds $1.50.)

items.q: Mei earns $20.00 an hour. One day she works 10 hours: 8 regular hours and 2 overtime hours at time and a half. What is her pay for the day?
items.e: Regular: 8 × $20 = $160. Overtime: 2 × $30 = $60. Total: $220.00. ($200.00 forgets the overtime rate; $300.00 pays all 10 hours at $30.)

items.q: A job pays a salary of $48 000 a year. How much is that per month?
items.e: There are 12 months in a year. $48 000 ÷ 12 = $4000.00 a month. ($4800.00 divides by 10; $2000.00 divides by 24, which is twice a month.)

items.q: A worker earns $46 800 a year and is paid every two weeks (26 pays a year). How much is each gross pay?
items.e: $46 800 ÷ 26 = $1800.00. ($3900.00 divides by 12, which is monthly; $900.00 divides by 52, which is weekly; $1950.00 divides by 24, which is twice a month.)

items.q: A job pays $20.00 an hour for 40 hours a week. What is the gross pay for 52 weeks?
items.e: One week: $20 × 40 = $800. One year: $800 × 52 = $41 600.00. ($800.00 is one week; $1040.00 forgets the 40 hours; $3200.00 is only 4 weeks.)

items.q: Tree planters in BC are often paid for each tree they plant. Emma earns 16¢ a tree and plants 1500 trees in a day. How much does she earn?
items.e: 16¢ = $0.16. $0.16 × 1500 = $240.00. ($24.00 and $2400.00 put the decimal point in the wrong place; $1516.00 adds.)

items.q: Hana sells bikes in Kelowna and earns 5% commission on her sales. She sells $6000 of bikes this month. How much commission does she earn?
Job A pays $17.50 an hour for 30 hours a week. Job B pays $480 a week. Which job pays more each week, and by how much?
items.e: Job A: $17.50 × 30 = $525. Job B: $480. $525 − $480 = $45, so Job A pays $45 more. ($462.50 subtracts the hourly wage from $480.)

items.q: What is the net pay on this pay stub?
items.e: Add the deductions: $118.20 + $63.39 + $19.56 = $201.15. Net pay: $1200.00 − $201.15 = $998.85. ($1081.80 subtracts only the income tax; $1401.15 adds the deductions.)

items.q: Lucas’s gross pay is $600 and his net pay is $510. What percent of his gross pay was deducted?
items.e: Deducted: $600 − $510 = $90. Compare with the gross pay: $90 ÷ $600 = 0.15 = 15%. (85% is the part kept; 17.6% divides by the net pay; 90% uses the dollars.)

items.q: Ethan earns $18.00 an hour. Last week his gross pay was $378.00. How many hours did he work?
items.e: Hours = pay ÷ wage = $378 ÷ $18 = 21 hours. Check: $18 × 21 = $378. (2.1 and 210 put the decimal point in the wrong place; 396 adds.)

items.q: Nadia’s wage goes up from $18.00 to $18.90 an hour. What is the percent increase?
items.e: Increase: $18.90 − $18.00 = $0.90. Compare with the old wage: $0.90 ÷ $18.00 = 0.05 = 5%. (4.8% divides by the new wage; 0.9% uses the dollars.)

items.q: Which of these is a fixed expense?
items.e: A fixed expense is the same amount every month. Rent is set in the lease. Groceries, movies and gas change with how much you buy or use, so they are variable.

items.q: Which of these is a variable expense?
items.e: Groceries change from month to month, so they are variable. Rent, a set phone plan and an insurance payment are the same each month, so they are fixed.

items.q: A student buys a monthly transit pass for SkyTrain and buses. It costs the same every month. What type of expense is it?
c: Fixed: the amount is the same each month
It is income, not an expense
Variable: the amount changes from month to month
It is a deduction from pay
items.e: The price of the pass is the same each month, so it is fixed, even if the student rides more in some months. (Calling it variable mixes up how much you use it with how much you pay.)

items.q: A family’s electricity bill is higher in winter and lower in summer. What type of expense is it?
c: It is income, not an expense
It is a deduction from pay
Variable: the amount changes from month to month
Fixed: the amount is the same each month
items.e: The bill changes with how much power the family uses, so it is variable. (Paying a bill every month does not make it fixed; the amount must stay the same.)

items.q: What is the total of Olivia’s fixed expenses?
items.e: Add only the fixed rows: $900 + $45 + $110 = $1055.00. ($1455.00 adds every row; $400.00 is the variable total; $1135.00 counts Entertainment as fixed.)

items.q: Arjun’s variable expenses this month are food $260, clothes $75 and fun $90. His fixed expenses are rent $850 and phone $50. What is the total of his variable expenses?
items.e: Variable: $260 + $75 + $90 = $425.00. ($900.00 is the fixed total; $1325.00 adds everything; $475.00 counts the phone as variable.)

items.q: A monthly budget has income of $2400 and expenses of $2150. What is the result?
items.e: Income − expenses = $2400 − $2150 = $250. Income is more than expenses, so it is a surplus of $250: money left over to save.

items.q: A monthly budget has income of $1800 and expenses of $1950. What is the result?
items.e: Income − expenses = $1800 − $1950 = −$150. Expenses are more than income, so it is a deficit of $150.

items.q: A family spends $90 a week on groceries. About how much is that per month? (Use 52 weeks in a year.)
items.e: $90 × 52 = $4680 a year. $4680 ÷ 12 = $390.00 a month. ($360.00 uses 4 weeks a month, but most months are a bit more than 4 weeks; $4680.00 is the whole year.)

items.q: Sofia’s monthly income is $3000 after deductions. Rent is $1050. What percent of her income goes to rent?
items.e: $1050 ÷ $3000 = 0.35 = 35%. (65% is the rest of the income; 28.6% divides the wrong way round.)

items.q: One budget plan is 50/30/20: 50% for needs, 30% for wants and 20% for savings. With a monthly income of $2800, how much goes to savings?
Liam spends $160 a month on entertainment. He cuts it by 25%. What is the new amount?
Monthly income is $2200 and fixed expenses are $1400. What is the most the variable expenses can be without a deficit?
items.e: Money left after fixed expenses: $2200 − $1400 = $800.00. Variable expenses must stay at or below this. ($3600.00 adds.)

items.q: Car insurance costs $1440 a year. How much should a monthly budget set aside for it?
items.e: $1440 ÷ 12 months = $120.00 a month. ($144.00 divides by 10; $360.00 divides by 4; $17 280.00 multiplies by 12.)

items.q: Which word belongs in the empty Type box for Food?
items.e: The amount spent on food changes with what you buy, so food is variable. Rent, internet and a bus pass are the same each month, so they are fixed.

items.q: Zara’s monthly income is $2000. Fixed expenses are $1200 and variable expenses are $650. She wants to save $250 a month. By how much must she cut her variable expenses?
items.e: Now: $2000 − $1200 − $650 = $150 left. To save $250, she needs $250 − $150 = $100.00 more. (Fixed expenses like rent are hard to change, so the cut comes from variable expenses. $250.00 forgets the $150 already left.)

items.q: A family’s grocery spending goes up from $400 to $440 a month. What is the percent increase?
items.e: Increase: $40. Compare with the old amount: $40 ÷ $400 = 0.1 = 10%. (9.1% divides by the new amount; 110% is the new amount as a percent of the old.)

items.q: A budget for a monthly income of $2500 uses 40% for rent, 25% for food and 15% for transportation. The rest goes to savings. How much is saved?
Mateo is paid $640 every week. About how much is that per month? (Use 52 weeks in a year.)
items.e: $640 × 52 = $33 280 a year. $33 280 ÷ 12 = $2773.33 a month (rounded to the cent). ($2560.00 uses 4 weeks a month; $7680.00 multiplies by 12; $33 280.00 is the whole year.)

items.q: Ji-woo earns $1000 a month. Fixed expenses: phone $55, transit pass $110, gym $35. Variable expenses: food $240, fun $180. She saves the rest. What percent of her income does she save?
items.e: Expenses: $55 + $110 + $35 + $240 + $180 = $620. Saved: $1000 − $620 = $380. $380 ÷ $1000 = 38%. (62% is the part spent; 80% forgets the variable expenses; 58% forgets the fixed expenses.)

items.q: A $30 adult phone case has 5% GST and 7% PST added. How much tax is that in total?
An adult bike helmet costs $45 before tax. 5% GST and 7% PST are added. What is the total?
Kai has $25. A video game has a price tag of $24. 5% GST and 7% PST are added at the till. Can he buy it?
items.e: Tax: 12% of $24 = $2.88. Total: $24 + $2.88 = $26.88, which is more than $25. No. (Forgetting the tax makes it look like $1 is left over.)

items.q: What is the total on this receipt?
items.e: Subtotal + GST + PST = $25.00 + $1.25 + $1.75 = $28.00. ($26.25 forgets the PST; $26.75 forgets the GST; $37.00 adds $12.)

items.q: A family’s restaurant meal in Nanaimo costs $36 before tax. Restaurant meals in BC have 5% GST but no PST. What is the total?
items.e: GST only: $36 × 0.05 = $1.80. Total: $36 + $1.80 = $37.80. ($40.32 adds PST too, but restaurant meals have no PST.)

items.q: A child’s winter jacket costs $45. Children’s clothing in BC has 5% GST but no PST. What is the total?
items.e: GST only: $45 × 0.05 = $2.25. Total: $47.25. ($50.40 adds PST too; $45.05 adds 5¢ instead of 5%.)

items.q: In Canada, which payment is rounded to the nearest 5¢?
items.e: Canada has no pennies, so only cash totals round to the nearest 5¢. Debit and credit payments are exact to the cent.

items.q: Harjot buys an $11.99 phone charger. 5% GST and 7% PST make the total $13.43. He pays with cash. How much does he pay?
items.e: Cash rounds to the nearest 5¢. $13.43 is between $13.40 and $13.45 and closer to $13.45, so he pays $13.45. ($13.43 is the exact debit amount; $13.40 rounds the wrong way.)

items.q: A $14.25 adult T-shirt has 5% GST and 7% PST added. You pay with a $20 bill. How much change do you get?
items.e: GST: $0.71. PST: $1.00. Total: $15.96. Cash rounds to $15.95. Change: $20.00 − $15.95 = $4.05. ($4.04 forgets the cash rounding; $5.75 forgets the tax.)

items.q: Adult running shoes cost $75 and are 20% off. 5% GST and 7% PST are added to the sale price. What is the total?
items.e: Sale price: $75 − $15 = $60. Tax: 12% of $60 = $7.20. Total: $67.20. ($69.00 takes 20% off and adds 12% in one step: $75 × 0.92; $60.00 forgets the tax; $84.00 forgets the discount.)

items.q: A $55 item has a $10-off coupon. GST and PST (12%) are charged on the price after the coupon. What is the total?
items.e: Coupon first: $55 − $10 = $45. Tax: 12% of $45 = $5.40. Total: $50.40. ($51.60 adds tax before the coupon: $61.60 − $10; $45.00 forgets the tax.)

items.q: You buy 3 notebooks at $4.25 each. 5% GST and 7% PST are added. What is the total?
items.e: Subtotal: 3 × $4.25 = $12.75. Tax: 12% of $12.75 = $1.53. Total: $14.28. ($12.75 forgets the tax; $13.39 adds only GST; $24.75 adds $12.)

items.q: A receipt total is $89.60. It includes 5% GST and 7% PST. What was the price before tax?
items.e: The total is 112% of the price. Price = $89.60 ÷ 1.12 = $80.00. Check: $80 × 1.12 = $89.60. ($78.85 takes 12% of the total, but the tax was 12% of the price; $77.60 subtracts $12.)

items.q: Store A sells a jacket for $120 plus GST and PST (12%). Store B sells the same jacket for $132 with tax included. Which is cheaper?
items.e: Store A: $120 × 1.12 = $134.40. Store B: $132.00. Store B is cheaper by $2.40. (Store A by $12 forgets to add tax to Store A’s price.)

items.q: You buy a pair of children’s shoes for $40 (5% GST only) and an adult shirt for $25 (5% GST and 7% PST). What is the total?
items.e: Shoes: $40 + $2.00 = $42.00. Shirt: $25 + $3.00 = $28.00. Total: $70.00. ($72.80 adds 12% to both; $68.25 adds only GST to both; $65.00 forgets the tax.)

items.q: Simran returns a $30 adult item she paid for with 5% GST and 7% PST. The store refunds the price and the tax. How much is the refund?
items.e: The refund includes the tax that was paid: $30 + $3.60 = $33.60. ($30.00 forgets the tax; $26.40 subtracts the tax.)

items.q: A phone costs $199.99. 5% GST and 7% PST are added, each rounded to the cent. What is the total?
Adult T-shirts are $15 each with a deal: buy 2, get the third one free. You take 3 T-shirts. 5% GST and 7% PST are added. What is the total?
items.e: You pay for 2: $30. Tax: 12% of $30 = $3.60. Total: $33.60. ($50.40 pays for all 3; $30.00 forgets the tax; $31.50 adds only GST.)

items.q: Jasleen buys a $96 adult hockey stick at 25% off. 5% GST and 7% PST are added. She pays with a $100 bill. How much change does she get?
items.e: Sale price: $96 − $24 = $72. Tax: 12% of $72 = $8.64. Total: $80.64, which rounds to $80.65 for cash. Change: $100.00 − $80.65 = $19.35. ($19.36 forgets the cash rounding; $28.00 forgets the tax; $16.48 uses $96 × 0.87, which mixes the discount and tax into one step.)

items.q: At a store in Prince George, Ava buys a child’s hoodie for $18 (5% GST only) and an adult cap for $20 (5% GST and 7% PST). She pays with two $20 bills and a toonie. How much change does she get?
items.e: Hoodie: $18 + $0.90 = $18.90. Cap: $20 + $2.40 = $22.40. Total: $41.30 (already a multiple of 5¢). Paid: $40 + $2 = $42. Change: $42.00 − $41.30 = $0.70. ($4.00 forgets the tax; $2.10 adds only GST to both; $0.85 puts the PST on the hoodie instead of the cap.)

items.q: Which transaction increases a bank account balance?
items.e: A deposit adds money to the account. Purchases, fees and withdrawals take money out.

items.q: A bank account has $285.00. A deposit of $145.00 is made. What is the new balance?
items.e: A deposit is added: $285 + $145 = $430.00. ($140.00 subtracts; $420.00 loses one carried 1 and $320.00 loses both.)

items.q: A bank account has $430.00. A withdrawal of $65.50 is made. What is the new balance?
items.e: A withdrawal is subtracted: $430.00 − $65.50 = $364.50. ($495.50 adds; $375.50 and $365.50 are regrouping slips.)

items.q: What is the balance after the ATM withdrawal?
items.e: Start from the last balance and subtract: $274.75 − $40.00 = $234.75. ($314.75 adds the withdrawal; $310.00 forgets the jacket; $465.25 adds every amount.)

items.q: A bank account has a fee of $4.95 a month. How much are the fees for a whole year?
items.e: 12 months × $4.95 = $59.40. ($257.40 uses 52, the number of weeks; $49.50 uses 10.)

items.q: A bank plan includes 12 free transactions a month. Each extra transaction costs $1.25. How much is charged for 17 transactions?
items.e: Extra transactions: 17 − 12 = 5. Fee: 5 × $1.25 = $6.25. ($21.25 charges all 17; $15.00 charges the 12 free ones; $7.50 uses 6.)

items.q: Noah takes $60 from another bank’s ATM. That ATM charges $3.50 and his own bank charges $2.00. By how much does his balance go down?
Wei’s account has $40.00. He makes a $65.00 debit purchase, and the account has overdraft protection. What is the new balance?
items.e: $40 − $65 = −$25. The balance is −$25.00: he owes the bank $25. (A positive $25.00 drops the sign; $105.00 adds.)

items.q: An account balance is −$25.00. The bank charges a $5.00 overdraft fee. What is the new balance?
items.e: A fee takes money away: −$25 − $5 = −$30.00. The account is now further below zero. (−$20.00 adds the fee as if it were a deposit.)

items.q: Plan A has no monthly fee but charges $1.00 for each transaction. Plan B costs $10.95 a month with unlimited transactions. With 15 transactions a month, which plan is cheaper, and by how much?
Plan A charges $1.00 for each transaction and has no monthly fee. Plan B costs $10.95 a month. For how many transactions a month is Plan B cheaper?
items.e: 10 transactions on Plan A cost $10.00, less than $10.95. 11 transactions cost $11.00, more than $10.95. So Plan B is cheaper for 11 or more.

items.q: Leah’s bank charges $1.50 for each e-transfer. She sends $40 to a friend by e-transfer. How much leaves her account?
items.e: The amount sent plus the fee: $40.00 + $1.50 = $41.50. ($38.50 subtracts the fee; $40.00 forgets it.)

items.q: A savings account pays 1.5% interest per year. How much simple interest does $2000 earn in 1 year?
Chloe’s online banking shows a balance of $512.40. A debit purchase of $85.00 is still pending and has not been taken off yet. How much money does she really have to spend?
items.e: The pending purchase will come out: $512.40 − $85.00 = $427.40. ($597.40 adds it; $512.40 ignores it.)

items.q: An account starts at $300.00 and ends at $245.00. During the month there was a deposit of $50.00, a withdrawal of $80.00 and one more withdrawal. How much was the other withdrawal?
items.e: $300 + $50 − $80 = $270. $270 − $245 = $25.00. Check: $300 + $50 − $80 − $25 = $245. ($55.00 is only the start minus the end; $105.00 forgets the $80 withdrawal; $85.00 swaps the deposit and the withdrawal.)

items.q: Owen’s account starts the month at $180.00. His pay of $420.00 is deposited, his phone bill of $55.00 is paid, and the bank charges a $3.95 monthly fee. What is the balance at the end of the month?
Mei has $150.00 in her account. She buys a $60 adult jacket by debit, and 5% GST and 7% PST are added. What is the new balance?
items.e: Total: $60 × 1.12 = $67.20. Balance: $150.00 − $67.20 = $82.80. Debit is exact, so there is no rounding. ($90.00 forgets the tax; $87.00 adds only GST.)

items.q: Emma pays $3.95 a month for her bank account. A student account has no monthly fee. How much would she save in 2 years by switching?
items.e: 2 years = 24 months. 24 × $3.95 = $94.80. ($47.40 is only 1 year; $7.90 is 2 months; $410.80 uses 104 weeks.)

items.q: What balance belongs in the empty box?
items.e: $195.40 − $48.65 = $146.75. Check the next row: $146.75 − $4.95 = $141.80. ($244.05 adds the purchase; $71.75 starts from $120.40 and skips the deposit; $141.80 is the balance after the fee.)

items.q: Hana’s account has $85.40. This month she pays a $45.00 phone bill, buys lunch for $12.60 by debit, gets a pay deposit of $236.25 and is charged a $4.95 account fee. What is the balance at the end of the month?
items.e: $85.40 − $45.00 − $12.60 + $236.25 − $4.95 = $259.10. ($264.05 forgets the fee; $269.00 adds the fee; $284.30 adds the lunch instead of subtracting it.)

items.q: Lucas saves $15 a week for 8 weeks. How much does he save?
Ethan wants to save $180 and puts away $20 a week. How many weeks will it take?
items.e: $180 ÷ $20 = 9 weeks. Check: 9 × $20 = $180. (160 subtracts instead of dividing.)

items.q: Nadia is saving for a $400 used e-bike and has saved $260. How much more does she need?
items.e: Still needed = goal − saved = $400 − $260 = $140.00. ($660.00 adds; $260.00 is the amount saved; $35.00 is the percent still needed, 35%, not dollars.)

items.q: Olivia has saved $340 toward a $400 goal. What percent of the goal has she reached?
items.e: $340 ÷ $400 = 0.85 = 85%. (15% is the part still needed; 34% uses the dollars; 60% subtracts 340 from 400.)

items.q: Arjun wants a $250 adult bike. 5% GST and 7% PST are added. He saves $30 a week. How many weeks until he can buy it?
items.e: Total: $250 × 1.12 = $280. $280 ÷ $30 = 9.33..., so after 9 weeks there is only $270. Round up to 10 weeks. (9 weeks forgets the tax or rounds down; 8 weeks forgets the tax and rounds down; 9.33 weeks does not round to whole weeks.)

items.q: Sofia earns $360 a week and saves 15% of it. How many weeks will it take to save $810?
items.e: Saved each week: 15% of $360 = $54. $810 ÷ $54 = 15 weeks. (2.25 weeks divides by the whole $360 pay; 54 is the dollars saved each week, not the weeks; 3 weeks uses $810 ÷ $270, the part not saved.)

items.q: Liam is saving for a $600 ski trip to Whistler. He already has $150 and saves $45 a week. How many more weeks does he need?
items.e: Still needed: $600 − $150 = $450. $450 ÷ $45 = 10 weeks. (14 weeks forgets the $150 already saved; 17 weeks adds the $150.)

items.q: $1500 is put in a savings account at 2% simple interest per year. What is the balance after 3 years?
items.e: Interest: I = Prt = $1500 × 0.02 × 3 = $90. Balance: $1500 + $90 = $1590.00. ($90.00 is only the interest; $1530.00 is after 1 year; $10 500.00 uses 2 instead of 0.02.)

items.q: Option A: save $25 a week. Option B: save 10% of a $280 weekly pay. Which option saves more in 12 weeks, and by how much?
items.e: A: $25 a week. B: 10% of $280 = $28 a week, which is $3 more each week. In 12 weeks: 12 × $3 = $36 more with Option B. ($3 is only one week.)

items.q: Many people keep an emergency fund of 3 months of expenses. A family spends $1850 a month. How much should the fund be?
“Pay yourself first” means saving before spending. Zara saves 20% of her $1250 monthly net pay. How much does she save in 6 months?
items.e: Each month: 20% of $1250 = $250. 6 months: 6 × $250 = $1500.00. ($250.00 is one month; $7500.00 is all the pay for 6 months; $6000.00 is the part not saved.)

items.q: Mateo works 12 hours a week at $18 an hour and saves half of his pay. How many weeks until he has $650 for a new laptop?
items.e: Pay: 12 × $18 = $216. Saved: $108 a week. $650 ÷ $108 = 6.02, and 6 weeks give only $648. Round up: 7 weeks. (6 weeks rounds down; 6.02 weeks does not round to whole weeks; 4 weeks uses the whole pay: $650 ÷ $216 = 3.01 → 4.)

items.q: A $600 phone can be paid for now, or with a plan of $28 a month for 24 months. How much more does the plan cost in total?
Ji-woo saves $75 every month. How much does she save in a year?
Kai has saved $520. He buys adult snowboard boots that cost $280 at 25% off, plus 5% GST and 7% PST, by debit. How much of his savings is left?
items.e: Sale price: $280 − $70 = $210. Tax: 12% of $210 = $25.20. Total: $235.20. Left: $520.00 − $235.20 = $284.80. ($310.00 forgets the tax; $206.40 forgets the discount; $276.40 uses $280 × 0.87, mixing the discount and tax into one step.)

items.q: A class of 24 students plans a field trip to Victoria on BC Ferries. The trip costs $185 for each student. The class raised $2400 and shares it equally. How much does each student still pay?
items.e: Fundraising for each student: $2400 ÷ 24 = $100. Still to pay: $185 − $100 = $85.00. ($100.00 is the fundraising share; $161.00 subtracts 24.)

items.q: Harjot has a summer job at $18.25 an hour for 30 hours a week. About 10% of his pay is taken off for deductions. He saves all of his net pay. How many weeks until he has $3000?
items.e: Gross: $18.25 × 30 = $547.50. Net: $547.50 − $54.75 = $492.75. $3000 ÷ $492.75 = 6.09, so 6 weeks give only $2956.50. Round up: 7 weeks. (6 weeks rounds down or uses the gross pay; 6.09 weeks does not round to whole weeks; 5 weeks divides by the gross pay and rounds down: $3000 ÷ $547.50 = 5.48.)

items.q: Simran earns $240 a week. Her fixed expenses (phone and transit) are $60 a week and her variable expenses are about $95 a week. She saves the rest for a $520 trip. How many weeks will it take?
items.e: Saved each week: $240 − $60 − $95 = $85. $520 ÷ $85 = 6.1, and 6 weeks give only $510. Round up: 7 weeks. (6 weeks rounds down; 3 weeks forgets the variable expenses; 4 weeks forgets the fixed expenses.)

items.q: Jasleen and Ava save together for a $1200 family gift. Jasleen saves $35 a week and Ava saves $25 a week. How many weeks will it take?
items.e: Together they save $35 + $25 = $60 a week. $1200 ÷ $60 = 20 weeks. (35 weeks and 48 weeks use one person’s savings only; 60 is the dollars saved each week.)

items.q: Noah’s monthly budget: income $1200, fixed expenses $450, variable expenses $380. He saves the rest for a $2000 goal. If he cuts variable expenses by $80, how many months sooner does he reach the goal?
items.e: Now: saves $1200 − $450 − $380 = $370 a month. $2000 ÷ $370 = 5.4, so 6 months. After the cut: saves $450 a month. $2000 ÷ $450 = 4.4, so 5 months. 1 month sooner. (Months must be whole, so round up each time; 0.96 subtracts the unrounded numbers.)
